lead: This unit explains how reinforced concrete is designed safely: how concrete and steel behave, and how the working stress, ultimate load and limit state methods turn loads and strengths into a design. After it you can design a singly reinforced beam by the working stress method, explain the limit state philosophy of IS 456, and compute characteristic values, design values and the stress block of a beam at collapse.
about: The unit starts with the materials: the stress–strain curves of concrete and steel and the numbers IS 456 takes from them. It then follows the history of design methods: the working stress method with its permissible stresses, the ultimate load method with its load factor, and the limit state method that checks both collapse and serviceability. The last three chapters give the tools of limit state design: characteristic strength and loads, partial safety factors and design values, and the stress block that turns them into a moment of resistance.

chapters.idea: The stress–strain behaviour of concrete and reinforcing steel sets the limits for every design method.
chapters.depth: Cover concrete grades M20 to M50, cube and cylinder strength, the nonlinear stress–strain curve, modulus of elasticity, creep, shrinkage and durability in brief. Cover steel grades Fe415, Fe500 and Fe550, the yield plateau, ultimate strength and ductility. Define fck as characteristic cube strength and fy as characteristic yield strength. Some syllabi call this material behaviour or stress–strain characteristics. Keep the design equations for later chapters.

figure.title: Stress–strain curves for M25 concrete and Fe415 steel
figure.aria: A plot with a curved concrete stress–strain line peaking near 25 N/mm² and a steel line rising to a flat plateau at 415 N/mm².

chapters.example: For M25 concrete and Fe415 steel, estimate the short-term modulus of concrete from Ec = 5000√fck and state the characteristic yield strength of the steel. Here fck = 25 N/mm², so Ec = 5000√25 = 25,000 N/mm². Fe415 steel has characteristic yield strength fy = 415 N/mm².
chapters.trap: Do not use the cube strength 25 N/mm² as the modulus of concrete, and do not treat 415 N/mm² as the design strength of Fe415 steel; it is the characteristic yield strength.
chapters.leave: Leave detailed mix design to concrete technology; leave design equations to Chapters 1.2 to 1.7 and beam design to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Working stress method keeps elastic stresses at service loads below permissible values.
chapters.depth: Explain the elastic or working stress method, often called WSM. State its assumptions: plane sections remain plane, concrete is linear elastic in compression, concrete carries no tension, and steel and concrete act together through the modular ratio m = 280/(3σcbc). Define permissible stresses σcbc and σst. Show the balanced section, neutral axis depth factor k, lever arm factor j and moment factor Q. Cover design of a singly reinforced rectangular beam by WSM. Keep the numerical beam design at the level of one simple section.

figure.title: Working stress method design check
figure.aria: A flow from service loads to elastic stresses, then comparison with permissible stresses, then fixing the section and steel.

chapters.example: A singly reinforced beam has b = 230 mm and d = 450 mm. Use M20 concrete with σcbc = 7 N/mm² and Fe415 steel with σst = 230 N/mm². Find the balanced moment of resistance and balanced steel area. m = 280/(3×7) = 13.33, k = mσcbc/(mσcbc + σst) = 0.289, j = 1 − k/3 = 0.904, Q = 0.5σcbc k j = 0.913. Mu = Q b d² = 0.913×230×450² = 42.5 kNm. Ast = Mu/(σst j d) = 454 mm².
chapters.trap: Do not use fy = 415 N/mm² as σst; WSM uses permissible stress, here 230 N/mm² for Fe415. Do not let concrete carry tension.
chapters.leave: Leave full beam design, doubly reinforced sections and flanged sections to Unit 2; leave shear and torsion to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Ultimate load method designs the section to resist factored ultimate loads at collapse.
chapters.depth: Explain the ultimate load method, also called ultimate load design or load factor method. Cover the idea of a global load factor, ultimate load, ultimate strength and collapse moment. Show how it differs from WSM: it checks collapse only and does not directly check service deflection or cracking. State its advantages and its limitations that led to limit state design. Keep the historical comparison brief.

figure.title: Ultimate load method
figure.aria: A flow multiplying service loads by a global load factor, obtaining ultimate loads, and checking collapse resistance.

chapters.example: A simply supported beam spans 6.0 m and carries a service dead load of 12 kN/m and a service live load of 8 kN/m. Use a global load factor of 1.5. Find the design ultimate moment. Total service load = 12 + 8 = 20 kN/m. Ultimate load = 1.5×20 = 30 kN/m. Mu = wL²/8 = 30×6.0²/8 = 135 kNm.
chapters.trap: Do not mix this global load factor with the separate partial safety factors of limit state design, and do not assume ultimate load method has checked deflection or cracking.
chapters.leave: Leave partial safety factors to Chapter 1.6 and serviceability checks to Chapter 1.4 and Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Limit state design requires safety against collapse and satisfactory behaviour at service.
chapters.depth: Define limit state as a state beyond which the structure no longer satisfies a design requirement. Cover limit state of collapse in flexure, shear, compression and torsion, and limit state of serviceability in deflection and cracking. Explain why limit state design is preferred over WSM and ULM: it checks both safety and service performance, and it uses partial safety factors. Some syllabi call this limit state philosophy or limit state method. Keep the probabilistic basis qualitative.

figure.aria: A tree splits limit states into collapse checks and serviceability checks.

chapters.example: A simply supported beam of span 6.0 m has a calculated total deflection of 28 mm. Check it against the IS 456 total deflection limit of span/250. Limit = 6000/250 = 24 mm. Actual 28 mm > 24 mm, so the serviceability limit is not satisfied.
chapters.trap: Do not treat serviceability as optional. Also do not use span/250 for every deflection check; it is the total deflection limit, while other limits apply after partitions and finishes.
chapters.leave: Leave detailed deflection calculation to Unit 2; leave beam, slab and column designs to Units 2 to 5.

chapters.idea: Characteristic strength and characteristic load are statistical values that define the design starting point.
chapters.depth: Define characteristic strength of concrete fck as the 28-day cube strength below which not more than 5% of test results fall. Define characteristic yield strength of steel fy in the same statistical sense. Define characteristic load as the load value with a small probability of being exceeded in service. Explain mean, standard deviation and the 5% fractile idea. Some syllabi call this characteristic values. Avoid deriving the statistics in full.

figure.title: Characteristic strength from cube tests
figure.aria: A bell-shaped distribution of cube strengths centred at 32 N/mm² with a marked lower-tail point at 25.4 N/mm².

chapters.example: Cube tests give a mean strength of 32 N/mm² and a standard deviation of 4 N/mm². Estimate the characteristic cube strength using fck = mean − 1.65σ. fck = 32 − 1.65×4 = 32 − 6.6 = 25.4 N/mm². This is rounded to the M25 grade.
chapters.trap: Do not take the average cube strength as fck. Characteristic strength is a lower fractile, not the mean.
chapters.leave: Leave load combinations and design values to Chapter 1.6; leave detailed statistics of loads to advanced study.

chapters.idea: Design values are obtained from characteristic values using partial safety factors for loads and materials.
chapters.depth: Define partial safety factor for loads γf and for materials γm. Cover common load combinations: dead plus live, and dead plus live plus wind. Give the usual material factors: γm = 1.5 for concrete and 1.15 for steel. Show design load = characteristic load × γf, design strength = characteristic strength/γm. Explain the concrete design compressive strength 0.67fck/γm, often written 0.446fck in flexure, and steel design strength fy/γm. Some syllabi call this design values and partial safety factors.

figure.title: From characteristic values to design values
figure.aria: Two paths convert characteristic load and characteristic strength into design values, then meet at a limit state check.

chapters.example: For M25 concrete and Fe500 steel, find the design compressive strength of concrete in flexure and the design yield strength of steel. Use γm = 1.5 for concrete and 1.15 for steel. Concrete: 0.67×25/1.5 = 11.17 N/mm², often taken as 0.446×25 = 11.15 N/mm². Steel: 500/1.15 = 434.8 N/mm².
chapters.trap: Do not multiply loads by γm or divide strengths by γf. Concrete and steel also use different γm values.
chapters.leave: Leave full load combinations to code reading; leave beam design using these values to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: The IS 456 stress block turns concrete compression at collapse into simple force and lever-arm terms.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Explain the equivalent stress block for limit state of collapse in flexure. Define xu as neutral axis depth, C = 0.36fck b xu as compressive force, z = d − 0.42xu as lever arm, and Mu = C z. Mention that 0.36 and 0.42 are stress block parameters, while the peak concrete stress in the block is 0.446fck. Use the steel force T = 0.87fy Ast. Do not derive the full parabolic-rectangular curve.

figure.title: Stress block parameters at collapse
figure.aria: A flow from the section to compression force and lever arm, then to moment capacity, with steel area from force balance.

chapters.trap: Do not use 0.446fck as the average stress in C = 0.36fck b xu, and do not use d in place of z = d − 0.42xu.
chapters.leave: Leave full singly and doubly reinforced beam design to Unit 2; leave stress block derivation to advanced study.
